summary: Specifies a distributed algorithm to divide a set of prefixes into unique, non-overlapping sub-prefixes assigned automatically. Combined with a protocol for flooding information, it can automate prefix configuration in a network.

plainLanguage.summary: Neighbors share out a big pizza so each gets a different slice and nobody ends up with the same piece.

questions: how are ip prefixes assigned automatically
what is the distributed prefix assignment algorithm
what does the apply timer do in prefix assignment
subtitle: A distributed algorithm that lets routers divide address prefixes among links without overlaps and without central configuration.

tldr.problem: Assigning non-overlapping sub-prefixes to the links of a network normally needs a central human or software authority.
tldr.mechanism: Each node shares its assignments through a flooding mechanism. Each assignment carries a priority, the highest priority wins, ties go to the greatest Node ID, and random backoff timers reduce collisions.
tldr.outcome: After a finite convergence period every link has at most one prefix per delegated prefix, none overlap, and assignments stay stable while topology and configuration do not change.

facts.label: Worst-case convergence
facts.value: 2 * Flooding Delay * L seconds (L = number of links)

today: RFC 7695 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it is still the specification of this algorithm.

sections.title: Introduction and Guarantees
sections.content:
RFC 7695 specifies a distributed algorithm for automatic prefix assignment, a generic alternative to centralized, human- or software-based assignment. It needs no configuration but accepts custom priorities, so it suits fully autonomic networks as well as configured ones. Picking a prefix value and length is context specific and out of scope.

Nodes advertise assigned prefixes through a flooding mechanism. An advertisement is a claim that the prefix is in use, and it tells other nodes which prefixes sit on their directly connected links. Given a set of delegated prefixes, the algorithm ensures that after a finite convergence period at most one prefix from each delegated prefix is assigned to each link, assigned prefixes do not overlap, and they do not change absent topology or configuration changes. The first two are the correctness conditions and the third is the convergence condition.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone announces which slice of the pizza they took. That way nobody picks a slice someone else already has, and slices stay put once chosen.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A Node runs the algorithm. A Link is what gets prefixes, either Shared (several nodes attached) or Private (an abstract link for private use or delegation, such as a DHCPv6-PD requesting router). A Delegated Prefix is the pool from which Assigned Prefixes come. The Flooding Mechanism reliably shares information, and its Flooding Delay should be an upper bound on propagation delay.

An Assigned Prefix is applied when it may be used for hosts, routing or delegation, and published when it is advertised. Each advertisement has a priority. In a conflict the greatest priority is kept, and a tie goes to the greatest Node ID. Adoption lets another node on the same link take over an advertised prefix after its advertiser stops, for example on node failure. Renumbering happens when an applied prefix is destroyed.

Node IDs must be strictly and totally ordered. How they are assigned is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A link is a table where kids sit, a published prefix is a slice you have called out, and an applied one is a slice you are really eating. Bigger numbers win arguments.

sections.title: Applicability Statement
sections.content:
The algorithm was primarily designed as an autonomic prefix assignment tool for home networks, but it applies elsewhere. It can run with no configuration, use advanced rules, work on any address space, and manage several spaces at once. For example, IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses allow IPv4 and IPv6 assignment from a single prefix space.

Every node MUST have a set of non-overlapping Delegated Prefixes, and the sets must eventually agree. All nodes MUST run a common flooding mechanism that carries each assigned prefix with its priority and the advertiser's Node ID, says which shared link it is on, and provides a Flooding Delay.

If the Flooding Delay holds and nothing else changes, renumbering happens only when a node deliberately overrides an assignment. Convergence then takes at most (2 * Flooding Delay * L) seconds, where L is the number of links. Joining nodes do not cause renumbering, departing nodes can be handled by adoption, but links that merge or split may. Because every node learns who made which assignment, the algorithm may be unsuitable where privacy among nodes matters.
sections.plainLanguage: It was made for home networks, but it works anywhere that everybody can shout to everybody else. Joining the game does not make anyone change slices.

sections.title: The Assignment Subroutine
sections.content:
The subroutine runs for each Delegated Prefix and Link pair whenever something relevant changes, such as an advertised prefix being added or removed, or a link, delegated prefix or Node ID changing. It also runs when the Backoff Timer fires with no Current Assignment. It first finds the Current Assignment and the Best Assignment, then acts on four cases.

  • Neither exists: if a new assignment is desired, wait a random backoff, pick a prefix that does not overlap any advertised prefix, and publish it with an Apply Timer of (2 * Flooding Delay).
  • Only a Best Assignment: copy it as a new, unpublished assignment.
  • Only a Current Assignment: destroy it if invalid. If valid and unpublished, adopt it, which SHOULD be preferred, or destroy it.
  • Both: if identical, mark the current one not published. Otherwise destroy it and take the best.

Two optional procedures let a node override existing assignments with a higher priority or remove a published one. They are allowed only after a configuration change, or after a link or advertised prefix is added or removed (overriding), so that convergence is kept. Other events are simple: the Apply Timer firing applies the prefix, and removing a delegated prefix or a link destroys the assignments in it.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want a slice, you wait a random moment so you do not grab at the same time as a friend. Then you pick a slice nobody has and call it out. If someone with a bigger number wants it, you give it up.

sections.title: Choosing a Prefix
sections.content:
The prefix for a new assignment MUST come from one of three sources: a prefix previously assigned and applied on that link (possibly kept in stable storage), a random pick from a set of at least RANDOM_SET_SIZE candidates, or a custom selection process from configuration. Picking randomly from all free space is simple but inefficient, since a few long prefixes can exhaust the short ones.

The optional efficient procedure weighs three criteria: stability across reboots, randomness, and address-space efficiency. It builds the candidate set from the available prefixes with the longest prefix lengths and prefers numerically smaller values on ties. It first reuses a stored prefix if possible, then tries a pseudorandom prefix based on node- and link-specific values, and finally picks randomly from the candidates. It can run in linear time, for example by keeping prefixes in a binary tree.
sections.plainLanguage: It is better to take a small slice from a corner already cut than to cut into a fresh, whole piece. That way big slices stay available for later.

sections.title: Behaviors and Parameters
sections.content:
Implementations can differ in capability and still interoperate. The RFC gives three example behaviors:

  • Listener: only acts on assignments by others and never creates or adopts any, suitable for lightweight devices.
  • Basic: assigns new prefixes and adopts non-conflicting ones, but does not override.
  • Advanced: also overrides and destroys assignments, useful when an administrator wants a particular prefix on a link.

The RFC gives no values for ADOPT_MAX_DELAY, BACKOFF_MAX_DELAY or RANDOM_SET_SIZE. Correctness and convergence hold for any values, even if they differ between nodes. They trade off convergence time, address efficiency, control traffic and collision probability. BACKOFF_MAX_DELAY MUST be greater than or equal to ADOPT_MAX_DELAY.
sections.plainLanguage: Some players only watch, some just pick slices, and some can ask to swap. They can all play together, and the timing numbers are left for each game to choose.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The algorithm depends on the Flooding Mechanism and the Node ID assignment mechanism. An attacker able to publish advertised prefixes could publish one overriding assignment for a whole delegated prefix or for the whole address space and so stop any assignment. The attacker could also add and remove advertisements quickly to generate flooding traffic and repeated executions, or to prevent convergence. Hiding advertised prefixes from nodes can break correctness, causing repeated Node ID changes costs traffic, and reusing another node's Node ID impedes collision resolution.

Where such attacks are possible, the subroutine SHOULD be rate limited.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad player could shout fake slice claims, or take over someone else's name, so everyone keeps rearguing. The fix is to slow down how often anyone reacts.
